text: Chapter 1 described data we already have. Chapter 2 flips the direction — probability describes what data we should expect from a process governed by chance. It's the language behind every later idea in this course, from sampling to hypothesis tests, and behind much of machine learning. This lesson builds the vocabulary, three rules, and uses simulation to check the math.

An experiment is any process with an uncertain result — rolling two dice, showing an ad to a visitor, checking whether a customer churns. An outcome is one possible result; the sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a set of outcomes we care about. The probability of an event A, written P of A, is a number from 0, impossible, to 1, certain. When every outcome is equally likely, probability is just counting favorable outcomes over total outcomes.

Roll two fair six-sided dice. The sample space is every ordered pair, so 6 times 6 equals 36 equally likely outcomes. Six of them sum to 7: one-six, two-five, three-four, four-three, five-two, six-one. So the probability the dice sum to 7 is 6 over 36, about 0.1667. The equally likely condition matters — applying this formula where outcomes aren't equally likely, like saying it either rains or it doesn't so 50 percent, is a classic mistake.

The complement of A is A does not happen, and since something must happen, P of not A equals 1 minus P of A. That's a huge shortcut for at-least-one questions. What's the chance of at least one six in two rolls? The chance of no six on one roll is 5 sixths, and the rolls are independent, so P of no sixes is 5 sixths squared, and P of at least one six is 1 minus that — both routes give 0.3056.

For A or B, add the probabilities but subtract the overlap so you don't count it twice: P of A or B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A and B. If A and B can never happen together, they're mutually exclusive and you just add. With one die, even and greater-than-4 overlap at 6, giving 3 sixths plus 2 sixths minus 1 sixth, about 0.667 — matching counting the union directly.

What does 0.1667 mean for a single roll? If you repeated the experiment many times, the fraction of times the event occurs would settle near that number — the law of large numbers. Simulating successively larger batches from a seeded generator: at 10 rolls we saw 0.2, at 100 rolls 0.17, at 10,000 rolls 0.1651, and at a million rolls 0.1665 — converging on the exact answer, 0.1667.

Small samples wobble — 0.2 is a 20 percent error — and large ones converge. The law of large numbers is about long-run fractions, not a promise that a short streak must balance out. After five losses in a row, the coin is still 50/50 on the next flip. Simulation is a powerful check throughout this course — when a formula is confusing, simulate the process and compare.

You can also estimate probabilities from data — if 12 percent of past customers churned, the mean of a 0/1 churned column estimates P of churn for a new, similar customer. That estimate is itself a sample statistic with uncertainty, exactly Lesson 1's theme. To recap: probability lives between 0 and 1, count favorable over total for equally likely outcomes, use 1 minus P of A for complements, and add minus overlap for or.
